<reason>PRO wins a well-matched debate on clash quality and burden control. CON's best weapons—policing the motion-shift in [B2.8], the share-of-revenue answer to budget caps [A4.1], and the "tautology" charge against counting only AI-created jobs [A4.5]—were all real, but PRO answered each one. B4.1-B4.2 recovered from the concession pressure by distinguishing jobs AI itself creates from economy-wide absorption, a textually defensible reading that blunts CON's net-vs-transition attack, and the closing crystallized the decisive question (cheaper cost center → margins or headcount?) with a concrete weighing: CON's elasticity loop was asserted while observable graduate hiring freezes run the other way. PRO's layered structure (asymmetry, satiated/budget-capped demand, entry-ladder hollowing, asymmetric policy error) gave multiple live routes; CON leaned almost entirely on the elasticity wall, which PRO contested plausibly every round. CON's opening was also clipped, a real execution cost. Neither side used fake sourcing, and both handled pressure questions with proper Q/A format; PRO simply made the debate easier to decide and left more paths standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1-B4.2 answering CON's motion-shift pressure: the "decade of churn" was a timescale challenge, not a concession, and jobs absorbing displaced workers need not be AI-created—directly defusing A3.1, followed by B5.1-B5.2's weighing that CON's demand loop was hypothetical while hiring freezes were observable.</best_rebuttal>
